news.title: Chuck Schumer dismisses opposition to his leadership from progressive Democrats
news.description: Chuck Schumer dismisses opposition to his leadership from progressive Democrats Submitted by MEE staff on Fri, 11/06/2026 - 17:26 Schumer says one of his most important Senate jobs is protecting US taxpayer aid to Israel US Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-NY) speaks at the Center For American Progress in Washington, DC, on 5 November 2026 (Tasos Katopodis/Getty Images/AFP) Off US Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer is facing opposition from progressives and a new group of Democratic lawmakers-elect to become Senate majority leader, in a rift that underscores the party’s divide on Israel. Senators-elect Adam Hamilton of Kansas, Troy Jackson of Maine, and Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan all said on the campaign trail that they will oppose Schumer as Senate majority leader. Meanwhile, progressive groups have said the Democrats’ sweeping midterm election victory on Tuesday should start the process of new lawmakers leading the party. “Voters made it very clear that they want a new generation of Democratic fighters,” Indivisible, a progressive Democratic group, said this week. “We need a Leader in the Senate who is capable of leading that fight. It’s time for Senate Democrats to choose new leadership.” One key difference between the 75-year-old Schumer and the new cohort of Democratic lawmakers is his position on Israel. Schumer is a longtime supporter of military aid to Israel and has manoeuvred to stop bills in Congress that would condition military assistance. In February 2026, Schumer said that one of his most important jobs as Senate minority leader was to “fight for aid to Israel”. “I have many jobs as leader… and one is to fight for aid to Israel, all the aid that Israel needs,” he told a group of pro-Israel Jewish leaders at the time. “As long as I’m in the Senate, this programme will continue to grow from strength to strength, and we won’t let anyone attack it or undo it,” Schumer said, even referring to US taxpayer aid for Israel as his “baby”. Schumer is Jewish-American and has received support from the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (Aipac). But recent polling shows that he is out of step with the majority of Jewish voters in the US, who lean heavily Democratic. Supermajority of Jewish Americans think Israel and Aipac drive antisemitism Read More » A supermajority of Jewish Americans think Israel and Aipac’s actions are increasing antisemitism in the US, a poll commissioned by J Street and published this week found. Still, the division on Schumer reflects a wider ideological divide within the Democratic Party. Senator-elect Sayed represents members who want to end the US’s support for Israel amid the genocide in Gaza and occupation of the West Bank. Other senators, like John Fetterman of Pennsylvania, are staunchly pro-Israel. But Schumer is likely to return as Senate majority leader, partly because no senior Democratic senators have expressed interest in the role. Schumer on Thursday dismissed talk of a rift within the party after a historic victory. "The bottom line is: first... we’ve had a very, very strong finish here, and I have worked really hard to get the results we got. But second, the issue is not me,” he told MS Now. “The issue is unity, fighting together. news.title: Democrats setting a veto trap for Trump with plan even some Republicans may back
news.description: Fresh off their sweeping midterm victory, Democrats are reviving proposals to raise taxes on the wealthy, and they don’t much care if President Donald Trump vetoes them. Ideas for a federal wealth tax and other steep tax hikes on the rich have been dormant for years, but Politico reported they're now “roaring back to life on Capitol Hill,” even as Trump promises to be “Mr. Veto.” Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-MD), a possible 2028 presidential contender, said Democrats should welcome a veto fight with a weakened Trump. “It is essential that we show the American people where we stand,” Van Hollen said. “If Trump vetoes it, it will just show people that he’s on the side of billionaires.” Democrats will take decisive majorities in both chambers in January, with far more room for error than Republicans have had over the past two years. Social Security’s looming insolvency, a $2 trillion deficit and pricey priorities like restoring health insurance subsidies will all have lawmakers hunting for revenue. Senior Democrats are already rolling out ideas. Sen. Chuck Schumer (D-NY), expected to become majority leader, recently proposed quadrupling a tax on stock buybacks. Sen. Ron Wyden (D-OR), set to retake the Finance Committee gavel, wants to restrict wealthy investors’ use of derivatives. Rep. Richard Neal (D-MA), the likely Ways and Means chair, wants to limit how much the rich can stash in retirement accounts. Van Hollen has also proposed surtaxes on people earning more than $1 million, and nearly half the Senate Democratic caucus has endorsed the idea, including moderates like Sens. Mark Kelly (D-AZ) and Angus King (I-ME). Democrats could get political cover from across the aisle. Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-OH) and Rep. Tom Cole (R-OK) have recently backed higher taxes to help fund Social Security, though both stop well short of supporting a wealth tax. A wealth tax itself faces a tougher road, Politico reported. Some Democrats worry the Supreme Court would strike it down as an unconstitutional “direct tax,” and California voters appear to have rejected a state version on Tuesday. It’s also unclear how the new red-state Democrats from places like South Carolina, Kansas and Iowa will vote on these proposals. “I don’t think we know yet,” said former Senate Democratic tax aide Anna Taylor. Alex Jacquez of the Groundwork Collaborative, which advocates for higher taxes on the rich, predicted that the incoming caucus will be friendlier to the idea than it was in the Biden years. “People are angry, and they are directing that anger at big corporations and the wealthy,” Jacquez said. “When it comes to public opinion, this is the best moment that you could have to raise taxes on the wealthy.”
